title: Circuit Design based on Feature Similarity for Quantum Generative Modeling
abstract_summary: The paper introduces a metric-based extension heuristic to design problem-informed quantum circuit topologies by measuring feature similarity, used to extend matrix-product-state (MPS) pretrained quantum circuit Born machines. Validated on the bars-and-stripes benchmark and a real-world Japanese government bond interest-rate dataset, the method reduces parameter count compared to all-to-all extensions and improves training performance and generalization over random circuit extensions, emphasizing the value of inductive bias in circuit design for quantum generative modeling.
methodology_description: The authors study quantum generative modeling using Quantum Circuit Born Machines (QCBMs) initialized by a tensor-network pretraining pipeline and subsequently extended by a problem-informed, metric-based circuit extension heuristic. First, a matrix product state (MPS) is trained classically with a DMRG-like algorithm to minimize negative log-likelihood (truncation cutoff 5e-5; 10 training iterations; learning rate 0.05). The trained MPS is analytically decomposed into a shallow PQC with linear connectivity. To capture correlations beyond the 1D MPS entanglement, they construct an undirected feature-similarity graph (vertices = features/qubits, edges = pairwise similarity) using either Hamming distance (for binary BAS images) or the standardized variation of information f_VI (for noisy/nonlinear financial data). A threshold (chosen via the elbow rule) determines which edges to add; corresponding SU(4) two-qubit gates (15 parameters, KAK decomposition into U(2) and RXX/RYY/RZZ) are appended to the decomposed circuit. Extension gate parameters are initialized near-identity (random normal mean 0, variance 0.01). The whole extended circuit is then retrained as a QCBM using stochastic gradient descent with ADAM as the optimizer. The objective is the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss estimated with a Gaussian-mixture kernel; gradients are computed via the parameter-shift rule (±π/2). Experiments compare multiple extension topologies (linear baseline, nearest-neighbor, metric-based, random with same parameter count, all-to-all) and report MMD on train and test sets over repeated runs.

experimental_setup: Numerical experiments run on the IBM Qiskit Aer statevector simulator. Two datasets were used: a 3x3 Bars-and-Stripes (BAS) binary image benchmark (9 qubits) and a real-world Japanese Government Bond (JGB) interest-rate dataset (5-, 10-, 20-year rates) preprocessed and quantized to 12 qubits (3 features × 4 bits).
dataset_used: Japanese government bond (JGB) daily interest rates for 5-, 10-, and 20-year maturities (source: Ministry of Finance Japan), period 2000-01-04 to 2025-02-28. Also used the 3×3 Bars-and-Stripes (BAS) binary image dataset (14 valid images).

JGB.raw_preprocessing: first-difference Dt = St - St-1 to represent daily changes and ensure stationarity
JGB.quantization: uniform quantization to n-bit binary via mapping formula; each of 3 features quantized to 4 bits (total 12 qubits)

pipeline_steps: Train MPS classically (DMRG-like) to minimize negative log-likelihood (truncation cutoff 5e-5; 10 iterations; lr=0.05).
Analytically decompose trained MPS to a shallow PQC with linear connectivity.
Compute pairwise feature similarity matrix (Hamming for BAS; f_VI for JGB).
Choose a threshold via elbow rule to build an undirected similarity graph; add edges where similarity indicates connection.
Extend the decomposed PQC by inserting SU(4) two-qubit gates on edges; decompose SU(4) via KAK into U(2) and RXX/RYY/RZZ components.
Initialize extension gate parameters near identity (normal(0, 0.01)).
Retrain the full extended circuit as a QCBM minimizing MMD loss with a Gaussian-mixture kernel; gradients computed via parameter-shift (±π/2); optimizer ADAM (stochastic gradient descent).
Evaluate MMD on train and test sets per iteration; repeat experiments (5 independent runs) for each circuit topology.

key_findings: [supported] A metric-based extension heuristic that connects qubits based on a classical feature-similarity metric (Hamming distance for binary toy data; variation of information for noisy/nonlinear financial data) can be used to extend a classically pretrained linear MPS-derived quantum circuit in a greedy, problem-informed way.

[supported] In numerical statevector simulations on the 3x3 Bars-and-Stripes (BAS) dataset (9 qubits), the metric-based extension (10 added two-qubit SU(4) gates) outperformed randomly chosen extensions with the same number of extra gates, and achieved better test-set MMD than an all-to-all extension (28 extra gates) which exhibited overfitting.

[supported] On a real-world financial dataset (Japanese government bond interest-rate changes), using variation-of-information to design the extension produced a circuit (12 qubits, 13 additional gates relative to linear baseline) that showed modestly better training-set MMD than random extensions in simulations.

[supported] Tensor-network (MPS) pretraining with truncation (cutoff 5e-5) provides a transferable baseline quantum circuit with linear connectivity; the MPS-trained solution was decomposed analytically into a shallow linear PQC that was then extended and retrained.

[supported] The metric-based extension materially reduces the number of additional parameters (and gates) compared to an all-to-all extension, enabling a tradeoff between inductive bias and circuit size under limited resources.

[speculative] The metric-based extension heuristic introduces useful inductive bias that may improve generalization in practice, but it is not guaranteed optimal and its effectiveness depends on chosen metric and threshold (no formal optimality guarantees).

[speculative] The approach may be practical for designing problem-informed circuits on near- and mid-term quantum hardware, but the present work used numerical (statevector) simulations and did not demonstrate results on actual noisy quantum devices.

[speculative] There is no established mathematical/theoretical connection in this work between classical feature similarity, entanglement capacity, and the circuit inductive bias — that remains an open research question (authors acknowledge limitation).

[supported] Different similarity metrics and thresholding (elbow rule) permit control over the number of added connections (inductive bias) in a greedy design process; this was used to select circuit extensions in the experiments.

[supported] Experimental setup details used in simulations: BAS experiment used 9 qubits, 1000 shots per iteration, 1000 iterations, 5 independent runs, training set 11 images / test set 3 images; JGB experiment used 12 qubits, 1000 shots, 1000 iterations, 5 runs, training set 4932 samples / test set 1233 samples.
results_summary: The paper proposes a practical, metric-based heuristic to extend an MPS-pretrained linear quantum circuit for quantum generative modeling by adding two-qubit SU(4) gates between qubits whose classical feature vectors are similar. In statevector simulations on the 3x3 Bars-and-Stripes dataset and on a Japanese government-bond interest-rate dataset, the metric-guided extensions (chosen via Hamming distance or variation-of-information and an elbow-rule threshold) consistently outperformed random extensions with the same number of added gates. The metric-based extension also used far fewer gates than all-to-all extensions and avoided the overfitting observed for the all-to-all case on the BAS test set. The work demonstrates that problem-informed circuit extension can introduce inductive bias while keeping circuit depth and parameter count manageable, but it is a heuristic without optimality guarantees and has not been validated on noisy quantum hardware.
performance_claims: BAS experiment: 9 qubits; metric-based extension added 10 two-qubit SU(4) gates; nearest-neighbor extension added 4 gates; all-to-all extension would add 28 gates. Training: 1000 shots, 1000 iterations, 5 independent runs. Train/test split: 11/3 images.

JGB experiment: 12 qubits; metric-based extension added 13 new connections (threshold 0.95 produced 21 total connections, 13 more than linear baseline). Training: 1000 shots, 1000 iterations, 5 independent runs. Train/test split: 4932/1233 samples.
MPS pretraining: truncation cutoff set to 5e-5; realized maximum bond dimension was 5 for BAS and 25 for the financial dataset in the classical MPS training.

Initialization and optimization details used in simulations: extension gate parameters initialized near identity (normal mean 0, std 0.01); optimizer: stochastic gradient descent with ADAM; MMD kernel bandwidth used: σ = 1.0 for BAS, σ = n/4 = 3 for JGB.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper discusses that quantum generative models may achieve advantages due to efficient sampling and expressive distributions, and argues that extending pretrained MPS circuits could be a route toward exploiting quantum resources. However, no quantum advantage is demonstrated empirically: results are from classical statevector simulations, comparisons are between circuit designs (not classical algorithms), and the authors explicitly frame the potential advantage as a motivation and future direction rather than a proven outcome.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Use MPS (tensor-network) classical pretraining followed by analytic MPS-to-PQC decomposition to initialize a shallow QCBM, reducing training burden on the variational circuit.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Introduce a metric-based circuit extension heuristic: build a feature-similarity graph (Hamming for BAS, standardized variation of information for JGB) and add two-qubit SU(4) gates along high-similarity edges to encode problem-informed inductive bias.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Metric-based extensions achieve comparable or better generalization (lower test MMD) with fewer parameters than all-to-all extensions and outperform random extensions, suggesting inductive bias can improve training efficiency in NISQ regimes.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Near-identity initialization of extension gates plus pretrained MPS leads to stable retraining of the extended QCBM, enabling workable experiments at 9–12 qubits on a statevector simulator.

#idea:hybrid-approach — KAK decomposition of appended SU(4) gates into U(2) and RXX/RYY/RZZ components enables implementation as parameterised two-qubit blocks compatible with PQC training and parameter-shift gradients.
